content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a unified pretraining framework that can handle 3D pose estimation, skeleton-based action recognition, and mesh recovery after simply fine-tuning. Besides, a novel encoder named DSTformer is also proposed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. The idea of handling 3D pose estimation, skeleton-based action recognition, and mesh recovery in a unified manner is interesting and the data resource heterogeneity problem that this paper aims to solve is also reasonable.
2. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
While I agree that it is important to build a unified model for human motion analysis, the main concern I have for this paper is the limited or incremental novelty. Below I will elaborate on this more.
1. With respect to the Dual-stream Spatio-temporal Transformer part, the authors simply propose to stack the spatial and temporal MHSA blocks in different orders and adaptatively fuse the output of the two branches. While this is kind of a reasonable idea to facilitate the learning process of both spatial and temporal information, my main concern is what is the difference between this simple idea and the other existing spatial-temporal transformers. Specifically, is there any special design in this Dual-stream Spatio-temporal Transformer that is relevant to human motion analysis, or what is the necessity of proposing a new spatial-temporal transformer encoder given that there is a lot of spatial-temporal transformer encoder architecture there already?
2. With respect to the design of the pretraining task, while I agree that there exists a 2D-to-3D lifting there, it seems that the major part of this designed pretraining task is "masking" and "adding noise". As these are quite typical pretraining techniques already, while I do find the design of the pretraining task reasonable, I have concerns about how novel is the design of the pretraining task in this paper.
3. With respect to the solution proposed for the data resource heterogeneity problem, which is to use the 2D skeletons as the universal medium, I also have the concern about the novelty as from my perspective, the usage of 2D skeletons in various human motion analysis subtasks has become quite common.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I believe that this paper is clear and much of its implementation details that are necessary for reproducing their method are given. However, as I mentioned above, I still have concerns about its quality, especially its novelty.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I believe that this paper focuses on an important problem and has proposed a complete and reasonable pipeline to solve this problem. However, my concern is that after I read into this pipeline, it seems that the novelty of each component of it is not enough for me. This is now the main reason for my hesitation about whether this paper should be accepted or not.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a unified model for multiple human motion-related tasks, which uses the 3D human pose estimation as the pretext task and proposes a dual spatial-temporal transformer as the motion encoder. The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performances on 3D human pose estimation and skeleton action recognition.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

(1) The proposed method achieves state-of-the-art performance on 3D human pose estimation and skeleton action recognition.

(2) This paper is well-written. 

Cons:

(1) From the reviewer's view, the proposed pretext task is the same as the pipeline for pose estimation. Therefore, it seems the proposed framework is a skeleton action recognition/human mesh recovery method based on the 3D pose estimation technique, which is not new. Additionally, the pipeline in Fig.1 (fine-tune) may be wrong, 3D pose estimation should be in front of action recognition and human motion recovery.

(2) When doing the skeleton action recognition, the input is the estimated 2D skeleton instead of the 3D skeleton, so it is not fair to compare the proposed method with the 3D skeleton action recognition methods. Additionally, the proposed method also includes extra training data. 

(3) The reasons for why using dual-stream are not well explained. The spatial-temporal transformer is not new for 3D human pose estimation and skeleton action recognition, while most works put the spatial transformer in front.

(4) Missing the comparison with a more accurate human mesh recovery method [1*-3*]. 

[1*] End-to-End Human Pose and Mesh Reconstruction with Transformers. CVPR 2021

[2*] PARE: Part Attention Regressor for 3D Human Body Estimation. ICCV 2021

[3*] Mesh Graphormer. ICCV 2021

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a Transformer-based architecture and a pretraining approach for learning representations for a variety of tasks, including 3D pose estimation, skeleton-based action recognition, and 3D mesh reconstruction. The proposed pipeline applies 2D-to-3D lifting to a sequence of noisy and masked 2D keypoints, which enables the model to learn geometric structures, spatio-temporal patterns, and motion dynamics. The pretrained model is then fine-tuned for the downstream tasks by leveraging limited task-specific data. The experiments show that this pretraining approach is more effective than training from scratch. The proposed model achieves better or competitive performance in various benchmarks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

1-	The proposed model and pretraining approach are evaluated and compared to state-of-the-art works in several benchmarks. In all cases, the pretrained and finetuned model outperforms the task-specific variant that is trained from scratch. This improvement supports the main motivation of the paper. 

2-	The DSTformer network seems to be very effective. Even when it is trained from scratch, it achieves slightly better performance than the baselines in the 3D pose estimation task and it is competitive in other tasks.

---

Weaknesses:

1-	The paper uses the "motion analysis" term quite often. However, a contribution to motion reconstruction is not demonstrated. An analysis of the quality of the predicted 3D poses or reconstructed meshes over time is missing. We do not know if there are any temporal inconsistencies or jitter. A supplementary video would also be helpful. 

2-	I find some inconsistencies in the reported benchmarks:

> a)	The 3D mesh recovery table (Tab. 3) doesn’t include state-of-the-art works such as [1*] and [2*]. More can be found at https://paperswithcode.com/sota/3d-human-pose-estimation-on-3dpw. Could the authors clarify if they followed the same evaluation procedure?

> b) In Table 2, the NTU-RGB+D results (left) for the baseline PoseConv3D are slightly lower than what was reported in the paper (see Tab. 8). 

3-	Similar dual attention/axial attention/dual stream concepts have been introduced in different but relevant domains. I think they should be discussed in the related work section and the novelties of the proposed DSTformer network should be highlighted. Some of the papers using this concept are [3*, 4*, 5*] and Zheng et al. (2021). 

4-	Finally, I have the following question: since the paper motivates learning a unified representation learning approach, wouldn’t it be better to use several objectives together, such as 2D reconstruction (i.e., denoising), 3D mesh recovery, and the next step prediction as in motion modeling? See [3*] as an example. After considering the missing baselines, the proposed approach seems not to be as effective in the 3D mesh recovery as it is in the other tasks. Could it be due to the pretraining objectives L_{3D} and L_{2D} which bias the model for the 3D pose estimation task?

5-	This is just an additional comment. I find the overuse of the term "motion analysis" a bit misleading. There is another line of research on the estimation of 3D pose and motion via physics-based approaches where the main focus is reconstructing 3D motion (see [6*] as a reference).

---

Additional References

[1*] Li, Jiefeng, et al. "Hybrik: A hybrid analytical-neural inverse kinematics solution for 3d human pose and shape estimation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021.

[2*] Lin, Kevin, Lijuan Wang, and Zicheng Liu. "End-to-end human pose and mesh reconstruction with transformers." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition. 2021.

[3*] Wan, Ziniu, et al. "Encoder-decoder with Multi-level Attention for 3D Human Shape and Pose Estimation." Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision. 2021.

[4*] Yu, Cunjun, et al. "Spatio-temporal graph transformer networks for pedestrian trajectory prediction." European Conference on Computer Vision. Springer, Cham, 2020.

[5*] Aksan, Emre, et al. "A spatio-temporal transformer for 3d human motion prediction." 2021 International Conference on 3D Vision (3DV). IEEE, 2021.

[6*] Shimada, Soshi, et al. "Neural monocular 3d human motion capture with physical awareness." ACM Transactions on Graphics (ToG) 40.4 (2021): 1-15.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and easy-to-follow. It is evaluated in various benchmarks and supported by ablations. The proposed network, DSTformer, follows commonly used dual attention concept over the temporal and spatial dimensions, but it introduces an interesting fusing technique (i.e., attention-based adaptive fusing).
content.summary_of_the_review: The network architecture and the pretraining scheme are simple yet effective. Despite the lack of technical novelty, the paper provides some evidence that it can be useful. However, I have concerns about the inconsistencies in the result tables and relatively poor performance in the 3D mesh recovery task. If the pretraining scheme favors one task due to the training objective (i.e., the 3D pose estimation-related terms in Eq. 8), then it is misleading to call it a "unified framework". I am leaning toward rejecting this paper after reading the current version. If the authors address my concerns and provide new evidence to support their claims, I would be willing to change my stance.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles various discriminative tasks for human motion including 3D pose/mesh estimation and action recognition. It proposes a pre-training routine with the objective of lifting 2D joints to 3D while at the same time denoising and filling in possibly missing joints. This routine is used to train a proposed “dual stream” transformer architecture for several downstream tasks. Experiments show that this pre-training improves the proposed transformer’s performance, especially in action recognition tasks, making it competitive with SOTA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* The idea of learning a shared motion representation that is useful across both pose estimation and action recognition tasks is appealing and intuitive since the tasks are so closely related.
* The experimental results are extensive. The action recognition results, especially in the one-shot case, interestingly show that learning a more 3D aware representation during pretraining is beneficial to this downstream task as indicated by improved performance over training from scratch, which makes sense.
* The ablation study shows that all components of the proposed pre-training routine are beneficial including the 3D task, de-noising, masking, and adding 2D data.
* Code is promised to be released for reproducibility. 

Weaknesses:
* Technically, the proposed DSTformer is a minor update to previous works, which already use alternating spatial and temporal attention, albeit in a “single stream” way [MixSTE, Zhang et al., CVPR 2022]. I am also not convinced the dual streams are truly a source of improvement: in Appendix Table 6, the single and dual stream architectures are compared with the same number of blocks (N) so the single-stream baselines will have fewer overall parameters. Moreover, the improvement for dual stream is only 1-2 mm compared to single stream. 
* Training on several heterogeneous data sources (both 3D and 2D) is already very common in 3D human pose/mesh recovery, which discounts the novelty and contribution of the proposed pre-training. 
* The baselines for human mesh recovery (Table 3), do not include any recent transformer-based models. For example, METRO [Lin et al., CVPR 2021] reports better results on both 3DPW and and Human3.6M than the proposed DSTformer method and already uses multi-dataset mixed training.
* For one-shot action recognition, it’s not clear where the performance boost in the “scratch” version of the model comes from. Is the contrastive training used by other methods? If not, is this the source of improvement or is it the transformer architecture?
* The ability for the pre-training method to generalize to other model architectures/methods is not shown. To see if this pre-training is useful even for architectures that already have all the “bells and whistles”, it would be good to see the SOTA approaches trained with the proposed method.

Questions, comments, and clarifications:
* The numbers for PoseConv3D in Table 2 don’t seem to match the reported results in that paper (Table 8)? Is the evaluation setting different here?
* Partial fine-tuning experiment (Table 5): Comparing a pre-trained backbone to a random backbone is not a very informative result. It might be better to instead include the non-frozen backbone result in Table 5 to more easily compare to how performance degrades when the backbone is frozen. 
* The paper tries to draw a parallel between the proposed approach and previous works that pre-train for other NLP/vision tasks, but I think this is a bit of a stretch since the pre-training task here is not simply self-supervised and instead relies heavily on detailed 3D pose annotations.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
In general, the paper is well written and clearly explained. Also, several implementation details are given and since code will be released the method should be reproducible.

Though the work does contain some novel components, I think the originality is hurt by the incremental nature of improvements. In particular, since mixed data training is already so common in 3D human pose estimation, the new parts of the proposed method boil down to adding masking and noise to pre-training, and the idea to fine-tune a 3D pose model for action recognition.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think the paper proposes an interesting idea and the results on action recognition are promising. However, as explained in the above, I think the contributions and novelty of the paper are much less than claimed and end up being a fairly incremental improvement over prior works both in the pre-training task and in the proposed model architecture. For this reason, I’m currently leaning slightly towards rejection.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a unified pretraining approach to learn from skeleton data in a self-supervised manner.  The pre-training pretext task requires the motion encoder to recover the underlying 3D motion from noisy partial 2D observations, e.g., 2D to 3D lifting.
The authors also design a Dual-stream Spatio-temporal Transformer network.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
$\textbf{Strengths}$

The paper is written well.

The method makes sense to me, and is in line with the current trend of self-supervised model pre-training.


$\textbf{Weaknesses}$

Firstly, I believe the work is slightly lacking in the novelty aspect. The pre-training method is straightforward, and the proposed Transformer seems simple.

Secondly, the design of the proposed Transformer needs to be better motivated, and the differences with respect to current spatial-temporal Transformer designs (e.g., [i],[ii]) needs to be well described.

[i] Decoupled Spatial-Temporal Attention Network for Skeleton-Based Action-Gesture Recognition. 

[ii] 3D Human Pose Estimation With Spatial and Temporal Transformers


Thirdly, as this is a self-supervised pre-training work, the “linear probe” self-supervised setting needs to be tested, and evaluated against current self-supervised representation learning methods (e.g., [iii]).

[iii] 3D Human Action Representation Learning via Cross-View Consistency Pursuit
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is written clearly.

The work does not seem very original or novel.

The paper seems reproducible as many details are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: Besides the fact that the novelty is slightly lacking, I believe that some important comparisons (w.r.t other Transformers and self-supervised representation learning methods) have not been conducted.
